title: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna
hook: black, then gray, then the color of a peach. the Rig Veda calls that hour a goddess

segments.voice: Yesterday, hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna, and the hymn to Indra that quotes its doubters: where is he? Did a doubt get said out loud before anyone answered it? Day one thousand two hundred seventy.
screen: `"WHERE IS HE?" AND THE ANSWER: TRUST.`

segments.voice: The window is black. Then, without any moment you could point to, it's gray. Then a thin band low in the sky turns the color of a peach. A bird starts. A car door shuts somewhere. A neighbor's light comes on. The day hasn't started yet, but everything is getting ready to. In the Rig Veda, this in-between light has a name: Ushas, the dawn, and she is a goddess. Today: the third of four voices.
screen: `BLACK, THEN GRAY, THEN PEACH.` → `EVERYTHING GETS READY.` → `USHAS, THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: Ushas is the dawn, and in the Rig Veda she's a goddess, pictured as a young woman in bright clothes, showing her brightness in the east. One hymn to her, book one, hymn one hundred thirteen, watches what she does to the world. In paraphrase: she wakes every living thing. She sends one person off to power, another to worship, another to seek a goal. The sleeper stirs. The one lying down gets up. The whole world, which had been still, starts moving again because she has come. Then the hymn looks at time. She follows the path of the dawns that have gone before, it says, and she is the first of all the endless dawns still to come. Every morning, then, stands in a line: behind it, every dawn there has been; ahead, every dawn there will be. Today's dawn is at the front of that second line. And then a quieter verse. In paraphrase: those mortals who saw the earlier dawns have gone. Now she is seen by us. And those who will see her in days to come are on their way. It's a hymn about the morning, and it doesn't look away from time passing. The people who watched dawn before are gone, and others will watch it after. The verse doesn't dwell on fear. Some readers hear company in it instead: the same dawn, seen by those before, by us now, and by those still coming.
screen: `USHAS: DAWN, AND A GODDESS.` · `SHE WAKES WHAT IS LIVING.` · `FIRST OF THE DAWNS STILL TO COME.` · `THEY SAW HER; WE SEE HER; OTHERS WILL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a small dawn, wherever you are. Sit, and if you can, face a window or any light. Close your eyes for a few breaths and let it be dark. Then open them slowly, a little at a time, and watch the light come in. Notice the first thing you see clearly. Then let your eyes rest half open. Bring to mind someone who saw many mornings before you, a grandparent, a teacher, anyone. And someone who'll see mornings after. Let them sit with you, one on each side. If you pray, you can offer the morning to them both. The bell holds the time.
Hymns to Agni, and today, to Ushas. The dawn goddess who wakes every living thing, the first of the dawns to come, seen by those before us and by those after. Today's word.

Your line: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna. Tomorrow morning, before the screen, look at the sky for one breath, and count yourself among the people who have seen it. Day one thousand two hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Hymns to Ushas are kept in Vedic recitation; in daily Hindu practice, some keep the hours before sunrise for prayer, bathing and the morning sandhya.

fork.setup: you're the poet, watching dawn and thinking of everyone who watched it before. what does the hymn do with that thought?
options: warns that every dawn brings death closer
names the past, the present and those to come
says this dawn is the last one
fork.reveal: it names all three: those who saw her are gone, we see her now, and others are coming who will see her.

original.note: Sanskrit: dawn, and the dawn goddess of the Rig Veda.

trapdoor: what you thought: a dawn hymn is about pretty colors.
what it means: Rig Veda 1.113 sees each dawn waking the world and standing in a line of dawns before and after.
what a scholar hears: the hymn calls her the first of the endless dawns to come, and sets the mortals who saw her before beside those who will see her after.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 1.113 (Ushas wakes the living; sends people to power, worship and their goals; follows the dawns gone before, first of the dawns to come; those who saw earlier dawns are gone, others will see her)

notes: RV 1.113 paraphrased from memory: waking the living and sending people to their tasks (around vv. 4–6, 9), 'following the path of dawns gone by, first of the endless dawns to come' (around v. 8), 'gone are the mortals who saw the earlier dawn' (around v. 11). Confirm each image and verse.
'Pictured as a young woman in bright clothes, showing her brightness in the east' draws on several Ushas hymns (e.g. RV 1.92, 1.123, 1.124); confirm the wording is acceptable for an app audience.

Editor pass: the hook's 'the poets watched this hour and gave it a name and a face' repeated day 1263's 'a Vedic poet watched this same hour and gave it a god', so it was reworded; 'one of them' (no antecedent) fixed to 'one hymn to her'; the errands in RV 1.113.6 brought closer to the text (power, worship, a goal); the closing reading ('it turns it into company') is now attributed to some readers; howItsDone 'often' softened.
